“Someone pointed out to me that the highest point of the Redeemer’s suffering, after the Agony in the Garden, must have been not the spitting, not the blows, not the scourging, not the crowning with thorns, not the carrying of the Cross, not even the Crucifixion, but simply appearing before a judge.”
Léon Bloy, Méditations d’un solitaire en 1916, 5th ed., Paris, c. 1920, p. 105.
“Pope Aenea Sylvio …” — This is not Aenea Sylvio Piccolomini, Pope Pius II, but his successor Pietro Barbo, who reigned as Pope Paul II from 1464 to 1471.
See Franz Xaver Seppelt, Das Papsttum im Spätmittelalter und in der Zeit der Renaissance (Geschichte des Papsttums IV), Leipzig 1941, p. 345.
Hefele — Karl Joseph Hefele, Conciliengeschichte. Nach den Quellen bearbeitet, continued by J. Hergenröther, 2nd improved ed., Vol. 1, Freiburg im Breisgau 1873.
Otto Veit — (1898–1984), ordoliberal economist, banker, and professor of economics and public affairs at the University of Frankfurt am Main.

Hauriou — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Maurice Hauriou, Principes de droit public. A l’usage des étudiants en licence et en doctorat ès-sciences politiques, 2nd ed., Paris 1916. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 27583.

with the Three Types and the Leviathan blurb — Carl Schmitt, Über die drei Arten des rechtswissenschaftlichen Denkens (On the Three Types of Juristic Thought), Publications of the Academy for German Law, Hamburg 1934.

The typed publicity sheet or blurb for Schmitt’s 1938 Leviathan book was circulated by Schmitt among various acquaintances after 1945 and has been reprinted several times, for example in Leviathan, pp. 243 f.
Whether it was actually written in 1938 is unclear.

an ambitious student of Thoma — Karl Schultes (1909–1982), Der Niedergang des staatsrechtlichen Denkens im Faschismus. Die Lehren des Herrn Prof. Carl Schmitt, Kronjurist der Gegenrevolution (Bausteine unseres neuen Weltbildes, 2), Weimar 1947.
Schmitt’s copy, containing annotations, inserted material, and pasted-in newspaper clippings, survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 28043.
Radbruch, Röpke, Böhm — Schmitt wrote to Radbruch on 13 September 1928:
“My engagement with you will proceed very slowly, because this is not a matter of cheap debate but of differences in our very modes of being.”
Schmitt later liked to sum up this difference—for example in his letters to Mohler—with the mocking phrase Homo homini Radbruch: “Man is a Radbruch to man.”
Material concerning Radbruch also survives in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 No. 21288.
Wilhelm Röpke (1899–1966), neoliberal economist, held Schmitt—and Smend—responsible for the collapse of the Weimar Constitution in his book Die deutsche Frage, 2nd ed., Zurich 1945, pp. 77 f.
Franz Böhm (1895–1977), jurist, economist, and politician, said at a Pestalozzi memorial event in 1946 that Pestalozzi’s attitude was completely different
“from that of almost every modern thinker of the state, beginning with Machiavelli and ending with the German constitutional lawyer Carl Schmitt and his power-worshipping disciples.”
Karl Geiler/Franz Böhm, Pestalozzi als Erzieher und Staatsdenker, p. 22.
See also the note below to p. 311.
Justus Koch — (1891–1962), lawyer and defense counsel in the Wilhelmstrasse Trial.
my memorandum from the summer of 1945 — Angriffskrieg (War of Aggression).
Dix — Rudolf Dix (1884–1952), criminal-defense lawyer. At Nuremberg he represented Hjalmar Schacht and Friedrich Flick. Schmitt had written the legal opinion mentioned above for Flick.
See Quaritsch’s afterword there: Angriffskrieg, p. 142.
Sciendum vero est … — “It must be understood that Satan’s will is always evil, but his power is never unjust, because he has his will from himself, whereas his power comes from God.”
Gregory the Great, Moralia in Iob, Book 2, ch. X, on verse 17.
Burckhardt’s opposite thesis — “And now power is evil in itself.”
Jacob Burckhardt, Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen, Kröner pocket edition 55, Stuttgart 1978, p. 97.
What Peterson says about clothing — Erik Peterson, “Theologie des Kleides,” in Benediktinische Monatsschrift 16, 1934, pp. 347–356. Also in Peterson, Ausgewählte Schriften, Vol. 2, Würzburg 1995.
Kempski — Jürgen von Kempski (1910–1998), philosopher. He studied under Carl Schmitt in the 1930s and repeatedly worked on Bruno Bauer.
Schmitt is probably referring to J. von Kempski, “Das kommunistische Palimpsest,” in Merkur, No. 7, 1948, pp. 53–68, where Kempski stresses Bruno Bauer’s decisive importance for Marx.

according to Barnikol — Ernst Barnikol (1892–1968), theologian. Schmitt is referring to E. Barnikol, Das entdeckte Christentum im Vormärz. Bruno Bauers Kampf gegen Religion u. Christentum u. Erstausg. seiner Kampfschrift, Jena 1927. Schmitt’s copy, with inserted material, survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 25529.

See also Barnikol, “Bruno Bauers Kampf gegen Religion und Christentum und die Spaltung der vormärzlichen preußischen Opposition,” in Zeitschrift für Kirchengeschichte 46, New Series 9, 1928, pp. 1–34.
Günther Krauss’s Captiva captivitas — See above, note to p. 93.
Maurice de Gandillac — (1906–2006), French philosopher, editor, and translator of the works of Nicholas of Cusa.

Schmitt owned Maurice de Gandillac, Nikolaus von Cues. Studien zu seiner Philosophie und philosophischen Weltanschauung, Düsseldorf 1953. Here, however, he is probably referring to the French edition first published in 1941.
Mittite me in mare … — Vulgate, Jonah 1:12.
“He said to them: Take me and throw me into the sea, and the sea will become calm for you. For I know that this great storm has come upon you because of me.”
a saying of Hegel — The quotation from Hegel’s Lectures on the History of Philosophy can be found in Nomos, p. 299.
Found the motto in E. Jünger — Ernst Jünger, Sämtliche Werke 9, Stuttgart 1979, p. 115.

“The year 1948 will give rise to many backward looks and renewed connections. The soil of German idealism seems to have contained something potent, and the rubble left behind by the skeptical break with it now seems to be turning into a field of ambiguous, rumbling beginnings of new theogonies.”
Schmitt to Rudolf Smend, 6 January 1948, in BW Smend, p. 121.

E. Rothacker — The philosopher Erich Rothacker (1888–1965) had known Schmitt since becoming a professor in Bonn in 1928. Their acquaintance probably deepened through Rothacker’s membership in the Academy for German Law and his role as a co-founder of the Committee for Philosophy of Law in 1934.

The handwritten draft of Schmitt’s letter to Rothacker survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 13429. The original is held by the Bonn University and State Library, Department of Manuscripts and Rare Books, Rothacker Papers.
Hans Barion wrote to Schmitt on 4 February 1948:
“Rothacker … spoke of you with great affection.”
conversation with Fr. Meinecke — Friedrich Meinecke had tried in 1922 to bring Carl Schmitt to the Deutsche Hochschule für Politik. See Tb 1921–24, p. 39. The attempt failed.
Nebel’s reflections on the elements — Gerhard Nebel, Von den Elementen, Wuppertal 1947. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 22280.
the little book Land and Sea — Carl Schmitt, Land und Meer. Eine weltgeschichtliche Betrachtung, Leipzig 1942.
Froude’s biography — James Anthony Froude, Lord Beaconsfield, Freeport 1971, reprint of the London 1890 edition.

The quotation containing the phrase “social sorcery,” which Schmitt repeated several times, does not actually come from the letter mentioned here, but from B. Disraeli, Tancred or the New Crusade, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1847, p. 252.
To Frau von Schnitzler — See Schmittiana, New Series I, 2011, pp. 182 f.
an overwhelming sentence from Saint-Martin — In the original:
“Pour prouver qu’on est régénéré, il faut régénérer tout ce qui est autour de nous.”
“To prove that one has been regenerated, one must regenerate everything around us.”
L. C. de Saint-Martin, Oeuvres Posthumes, Vol. 1, Tours 1807, p. 102.
See also Karl Epting, “Die politische Theologie Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin’s,” in Epirrhosis. Festgabe für Carl Schmitt, ed. Hans Barion et al., 2nd ed., Berlin 2002, pp. 161–184.

the speech written by Sallust — When the Roman Senate was debating what to do with the arrested Catilinarian conspirators, Caesar, in the speech recorded by Sallust, urged the senators to free themselves “from hatred and affection, anger and pity.”
“When a man exerts his rational judgment, it can achieve something; but when passion takes possession of him, passion rules, and reason is powerless.”
Gaius Sallustius Crispus, Die Verschwörung des Catilina, Latin and German, translated and annotated by Josef Lindauer, Reinbek 1964, pp. 64 ff.
lex Porcia — In his speech, Caesar cites the Porcian law, which forbade Roman officials to flog or execute a Roman citizen while ignoring his right to appeal to the popular assembly.
ne plus valeat apud vos illorum scelus … — In the original:
… ne plus apud vos valeat P. Lentuli et ceterorum scelus quam vostra dignitas, neu magis irae vostrae quam famae consulatis.
“… so that the crime of Publius Lentulus and the others does not carry more weight with you than your own dignity, and so that you do not pay more attention to your anger than to your good name.”
Don Capisco’s Pocket Oracle — Schmitt seems first to have used the name “Don Capisco” for himself in 1943.
On 24 January 1943, Ernst Jünger recorded a conversation with Carl Schmitt in which he “admired, or perhaps doubted, his expertise.”
“Don’t you know that I am Don Capisco?”
E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, Vol. 2, p. 487.

The manuscript originally contained the word “Gracián’s,” which was crossed out and replaced with “Don Capisco.” This indicates that Schmitt was placing himself in the tradition of the Spanish neo-Stoic writer Baltasar Gracián, who published his maxims under the title Handorakel und die Kunst der Weltklugheit—The Pocket Oracle and Art of Worldly Wisdom.
In Gracián’s novel The Criticón, the rational and discerning figure of Critilo was probably Schmitt’s model for Don Capisco.
to Scheffer — Paul Scheffer (1883–1963), journalist. On Schmitt’s long relationship with him, see Tb 1921–24, p. 71 and passim.
After leaving for the United States in 1937, Scheffer never returned to Germany.
Poor Jünger — Apparently refers to Ernst Jünger’s Strahlungen, which Schmitt had received in manuscript from Gerhard Nebel, as well as Jünger’s plans for Heliopolis.
Sent Ernst Jünger — See BW EJ, pp. 226 f.
Hamburg conference of German law professors — This means the meeting of the German Society for International Law, which had been dissolved in 1934 and re-established in 1947.
The 1948 meeting dealt with fundamental questions of international law, including the question of whether Germany had continued to exist as a subject of international law.
See Michael Stolleis, Geschichte des öffentlichen Rechts in Deutschland, Vol. 4, Munich 2012, pp. 76 ff.
Machiavelli says — Niccolò Machiavelli, Discorsi. Gedanken über Politik und Staatsführung, Kröner pocket edition 377, 3rd improved ed., Stuttgart 2007, p. 262.
Schmitt used the Testina edition of Tutte le opere from 1550, which is why the wording does not match.
Theodor Haecker said in 1917 … — Haecker actually wrote this as early as 1915: Theodor Haecker, “Der Krieg und die Führer des Geistes,” in Brenner-Jahrbuch 1915, pp. 130–188, here p. 170.
Schmitt probably gives the year as 1917 because the text was republished in Haecker’s Satire und Polemik in 1922 with an afterword dated 1917.

Haecker’s essay was a fierce attack on the intellectuals who supported the First World War. It was so sharp that it became a subject of debate in the Reichstag, and Der Brenner was subsequently banned.

Among other people, Haecker attacked Theodor Wolff, editor-in-chief of the Berliner Tageblatt. Wolff had written of the “sincere grief” felt by educated Germans over the destruction of cathedrals during the war.
